## What is a linkage?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Bars** are stiff. **Pivots** (pins) let them turn.
- Join bars with pivots, and one motor can move everything.
- A **parallelogram** has two equal bars, the same distance apart at both ends.
- Lift a parallelogram, and the far end **stays level**. That's why robot arms use them.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Parallelograms are everywhere:**

- robot lifts and arms
- a desk lamp
- a fold-out toolbox tray
- a bike's gear changer
- a car jack and a scissor lift
:::
::::

## The 4-bar lift {#four-bar}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/lifts.html?mode=four" title="4-bar lift"></iframe>

::: notes
Press **Lift**, or drag the **Lift** slider. Point out:

- The claw (and the yellow cube) **stays level** the whole time: the two blue bars are a parallelogram.
- The pink dotted line is the claw's path: an **arc**. The claw moves forward, then back, as it goes up. Ask: *why could that be a problem near a goal?*
- Change the **bar length**: longer bars lift higher, but need more motor power (or rubber bands to help).
:::

## The 6-bar lift {#six-bar-lift}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/lifts.html?mode=six" title="6-bar lift"></iframe>

::: notes
Two 4-bars that **share a bar**: 6 bars in all (count them with the class: tower, purple, blue, green, orange, and the claw's end bar).

- The first 4-bar's **top bar is twice as long** (purple). It keeps going and becomes the second 4-bar's bottom bar.
- The first 4-bar's **end bar is extra tall** (green). It crosses the purple bar (the X) and is the "tower" for the second 4-bar's top bar (orange).

Both 4-bars tilt together, so it lifts **about twice as high** as a 4-bar with the same bars, and the claw stays level. But it also reaches **further forward** as it goes up: on a small robot, it can tip over. Lower it all the way: that folded shape is how VEX shows it.
:::

## The DR4B: straight up {#dr4b}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/lifts.html?mode=dr4b" title="DR4B lift"></iframe>

::: notes
**DR4B** = double reverse four-bar. The top 4-bar tilts the **other way**, so the sideways movements cancel out and the claw goes **straight up** ("Claw moves forward: 0 cm"). The purple arrow and the box at the top right show the **extension**: how far the claw has gone up from its lowest point. The ruler on the left is in cm.

Ask: *Make the bars longer: how does the extension change?* (Each stage adds about bar length × the change in height, so two stages double it.) Real DR4Bs use rubber bands to help hold the weight up.
:::

## Lift words

::: {.matching}
- parallelogram | Two equal bars, the same distance apart at both ends
- pivot | A pin where a bar can turn
- 4-bar | One parallelogram: the claw goes up in an arc
- 6-bar | Two 4-bars sharing a long bar: about twice as high
- DR4B | The top 4-bar tilts back: the claw goes straight up
- extension | How far the claw goes up from its lowest point
:::

## Three ways to launch {#catapult}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/catapult.html?mode=slip" title="Catapult mechanisms"></iframe>

::: notes
Every rubber-band catapult has the same problem: **pull the arm back** (stretching the rubber band), **hold it**, then **let go** all at once. The buttons at the top show three ways. Use **Slow motion** to watch the release.

- **Slip gear**: a gear with some teeth cut off, turned by a motor. The teeth pull the arm back; when the gap comes round, the arm is free. It fires again and again by itself. (A common robot-competition launcher.)
- **Snail cam**: a spiral-shaped wheel. It pushes the arm's tail further and further, then the tail drops off the step. Also automatic.
- **Winch, latch and trigger**: wind the arm back with a string, hook it with a latch, let the string go slack, then pull the trigger. You choose *when* it fires.

All three need a **stop bar**: it stops the arm, and the ball keeps going. Ask: *what happens if the stop bar is lower? Higher?* (The ball flies flatter or higher.)
:::

## Which launcher is it?

::: {.sort}
- **Slip gear**
  - Some teeth are cut off | A slip gear is a normal gear with a gap where some teeth were.
  - Its teeth turn the arm's gear | The motor's gear turns the arm's gear, pulling the arm back.
- **Snail cam**
  - A spiral-shaped wheel with a step | A snail cam gets wider and wider, then has a sharp step.
  - The arm's tail drops off a step | When the tail falls off the step, the arm is free.
- **Latch and trigger**
  - A hook holds the arm | The latch hooks the arm, so the string can go slack.
  - You choose exactly when it fires | Pull the trigger when you're ready: the other two fire by themselves.
:::

## Build challenge: pull back and release

1. Make the **arm** and the **pivot**. Add a **stop bar** where the arm should stop.
2. Add **rubber bands** that stretch when the arm goes back.
3. Choose a way to **pull back and hold**: a slip gear, a snail cam, or a winch and a latch.
4. Test it. Change **one thing** at a time: the number of rubber bands, the stop bar, the pull-back angle.
5. Record how far the ball goes. Which change made the biggest difference?

::: notes
Tips: tie rubber bands to strong points, not thin parts. A sharp step on a cam (or a clean gap on a slip gear) releases cleanly. Keep fingers away from the arm when it's pulled back.
:::

## Going further: for the teacher {#going-further}

The next slides are the engineering behind it all: **general four-bar linkages** (crank, coupler and rocker), **Grashof's rule** for when a link can turn all the way round, and the **Watt** and **Stephenson** six-bar linkages.

::: notes
These are pitched above middle school. Use them for your own background, or for strong students who ask "why".
:::

## A general four-bar linkage {#four-bar-general}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/linkage.html?mode=four" title="Four-bar linkage"></iframe>

::: notes
Not a parallelogram: four links of different lengths. The crank (blue) turns; the rocker (green) swings; the pink path is drawn by point **P** on the coupler, and different points draw different curves. Windshield wipers, oil pump "nodding donkeys" and your leg on a bike pedal are four-bars like this.

Try the buttons on the right:

- **Crank-rocker**: the crank goes all the way round; the rocker swings.
- **Double-crank**: make the ground the shortest link, and *both* sides turn fully.
- **Double-rocker**: the coupler is shortest; the crank only rocks. Watch it hit its limit and turn back.
- **Parallelogram**: the robot-lift shape. The coupler stays level.
- **Straight line**: Hoeken's linkage. P moves in an almost straight line for part of the turn.
:::

## Grashof's rule

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Add the **shortest** and the **longest** link.

- If that is **less than or equal to** the other two added together, at least one link can turn **all the way round**.
- If it is **more**, no link can turn all the way. Everything only rocks.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Example:** 1, 4, 3 and 3.5

shortest + longest = 1 + 4 = **5**

the other two = 3 + 3.5 = **6.5**

5 ≤ 6.5, so one link turns fully ✓
:::
::::

::: notes
The simulator checks this rule live as you change the lengths. **Which** link turns fully depends on which link is the shortest: the crank (crank-rocker), the ground (double-crank) or the coupler (double-rocker: the coupler spins, but the crank and rocker only swing).
:::

## Will the crank turn all the way round?

::: {.sort}
- **Yes, it turns fully**
  - Crank 1, coupler 4, rocker 3, ground 3.5 | 1 + 4 = 5 ≤ 3 + 3.5 = 6.5, and the crank is the shortest link.
  - Crank 2, coupler 5, rocker 4, ground 4 | 2 + 5 = 7 ≤ 4 + 4 = 8, and the crank is the shortest link.
  - Crank 1.5, coupler 3, rocker 3, ground 2 | 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 ≤ 3 + 2 = 5, and the crank is the shortest link.
- **No, it only rocks**
  - Crank 3, coupler 3, rocker 3, ground 4 | 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 3 + 3 = 6: no link turns fully.
  - Crank 4, coupler 2, rocker 4, ground 5 | 2 + 5 = 7 ≤ 4 + 4 = 8, but the coupler is the shortest, so the crank only rocks.
  - Crank 3, coupler 5, rocker 2, ground 4.5 | 2 + 5 = 7 ≤ 3 + 4.5 = 7.5, but the rocker is the shortest: the rocker turns, not the crank.
:::

## Watt and Stephenson six-bars {#six-bar}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/linkage.html?mode=watt" title="Six-bar linkage"></iframe>

::: notes
A **six-bar** adds two more links (orange) and a third ground pivot. The extra links let one motor do more: a bigger swing, a pause, or a more complicated path.

- **Watt** (shown first): two four-bars in a row. The rocker is a three-joint piece (the green triangle), and it drives the second four-bar.
- **Stephenson** (button at the top): the extra links hang from the path point P on the coupler, so F follows a new path.

Real six-bars: car suspensions, excavator buckets, many walking robots, and the legs of Theo Jansen's walking Strandbeest sculptures.
:::

## Design your own

- **PMKS+**: design and test planar linkages in the browser, with paths, speeds and forces. [pmksplus.com](https://pmksplus.com){target="_blank"}
- **MotionGen**: draw linkages and make them follow a path you choose; free, on the web and on tablets. [motiongen.io](https://motiongen.io){target="_blank"}
- **Linkage** (free Windows program): quick sketches of linkages that move. [Linkage Mechanism Designer](https://blog.rectorsquid.com/linkage-mechanism-designer-and-simulator/){target="_blank"}
- **GeoGebra**: search "four-bar linkage" on geogebra.org for many ready-made models.

::: notes
These are outside tools (they need the internet). The lifts, catapults and linkage simulator in this deck are saved in the course (`embeds/`), so they work offline.
:::
